chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Ibn Faddal, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
"Standing at al-Mash'ar is an obligation (fard), and standing at 'Arafah is a sunnah."

What we mentioned is not contradicted, because the meaning of this report is that its obligation was known from the side of the Sunnah, not from the explicit text of the Quran. And whatever its obligation is known from the side of the Sunnah, it is permissible to be called by the name of 'Sunnah', and we have explained this in other places.
But it is not so for standing at al-Mash'ar, because its obligation is known from the explicit text of the Quran.
Allah, the Exalted, said: "So when you have departed from 'Arafat, remember Allah at al-Mash'ar al-Haram."

So He made it obligatory upon us to remember Him at al-Mash'ar al-Haram, and there was no command in the explicit text of the Quran regarding standing at 'Arafat; therefore, for that reason, it was attributed to the Sunnah.

As for that which indicates that standing at al-Mash'ar al-Haram is an obligation, it is the Verse and the preceding report as well, which is His saying: "Standing at al-Mash'ar is an obligation." And to add clarity to that is what was narrated:

key_terms.اَلْمَشْعَرُ: Al-Mash'ar (the place of standing, specifically al-Mash'ar al-Haram)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between the legal status of standing at 'Arafah and standing at al-Mash'ar during Hajj?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights a nuanced Shia jurisprudential distinction where the obligation of standing at 'Arafah is derived from the Sunnah rather than an explicit Quranic command, whereas standing at al-Mash'ar al-Haram is a direct Quranic injunction. This classification underscores the Shia methodology of distinguishing between *Fard* (obligatory) and *Sunnah* based on the primary source of evidence, reinforcing the authority of the Imams in interpreting ritual law. The text further links the Quranic command to remember God at al-Mash'ar with the Prophetic tradition, illustrating the interplay between textual revelation and transmitted practice.
